newsitem.title: HONG KONG: FUND VIEW - Competition spurs deregulation in 97.
newsitem.headline: FUND VIEW - Competition spurs deregulation in 97.

text.p: As Hong Kong prepares for its mid-1997 handover to China, financial market regulators in other Asian cities are searching for ways to attract the millions of investments dollars flowing into the region.
Most analysts and fund managers expect the British colony to remain an attractive investment centre, and many forecast continued gains in the Hang Seng Index in 1997.

But the old battle between Hong Kong and Singapore for the title of "The" financial centre in Asia will continue, with others, including Malaysia and the Philippines, throwing their hats into what they believe will be a very lucrative ring.
"We're going to go for it," Philippine Finance Secretary Roberto do Ocampo said recently in Manila when asked how ready the country was to become a regional financial centre.

Perhaps the most dramatic changes in the region will take place in Japan, where Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto has unveiled plans for a five-year "Big Bang" to liberalise the country's financial markets by 2001.
Although financial experts and analysts welcome the proposals, they say the prime minister will find rapid changes to the current system hard to implement.
Rather, the financial system overhaul will proceed at a gradual pace, they said.
"I don't think Japan can do everything in five years," Takashi Kanasaki, a director at Yamaichi Securities Co Ltd in Tokyo said recently of the time frame for "Big Bang".
Japan is not alone in experiencing a slow pace of change.
While many countries look to foreign funds to bolster their economies, they remain wary of opening their markets to widely and too quickly for fear of loosing control over their markets.
Singapore made several moves at deregulation in 1996-- announcing freer markets in telecommunications and financial services. But economists say the city-state remains tightly regulated.
Strict rules prevent most foreign banks from offering full services and restricted licensing effectively bars new foreign institutions from entering the insurance and pensions industries.
"There haven't been may advances," said Desmond Supple, senior emerging markets economist at consultancy I.D.E.A. "The trend is gradual, but Singapore has a long way to go," he said.
"Singapore's rivals in the region are growing their financial sectors fast and Singapore is going to have to run faster and faster to stand still in the industry," he added.
In neighbouring Malaysia, the government took a number of steps in 1996 to claim the title of regional financial centre -- a direction it plans to continue to follow in 1997.

It has also taken care to develop its offshore financial centre, officially called the Labuan International Offshore Financial Centre, which it sees as the global centre for islamic capital market activities.

In his 1997 budget speech, Finance Minister and Deputy Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said stockbrokers would be allowed to set up unit trusts, undertake fund management and underwriting, issue call warrants and manage listing of companies.
Foreign brokerages can take up to a 49 percent stake in local brokerage firms, but as of now cannot open offices without local participation.

South Korea raised the foreign stock ownership limit to 18 percent in April from 15 percent, and then to 20 percent in October. It plans to raise the foreign ceiling for equities by three percent every year from 1997 and abolish it by 2000.
Foreign investment trusts were allowed in December to open a joint venture with local firms.
In 1997, foreigners would be allowed to invest in long-term bonds issued by small and medium companies.

The finance ministry is also considering abandoning a paid-in capital requirement for foreign banks opening branches in South Korea, but there is no timetable yet for action. Currently, South Korea allows banks belonging to the world's top 500 to open a branch.
As part of its plans "to go for it," the Philippine government wants to open up the retail trade sector and raise the foreign equity limit in investment houses to 60 percent from 40 percent.
These are under discussion in the Philippine congress.

To develop its capital markets, the Philippines is also set to put in place a central depository system and the scripless trading of stocks. Its Securities and Exchange Commission will also implement a full-disclosure system.
"The government is going to push for liberalisation, privatisation and deregulation. These are the measures we have identified now," Assistant Finance Secretary Gil Beltran said.
"The Philippines will be more attractive to investors," he added.
